question.prompt:
A square with side length \(8\) is colored white except for \(4\) black isosceles right triangular regions with legs of length \(2\) in each corner of the square and a black diamond with side length \(2\sqrt{2}\) in the center of the square, as shown in the diagram.

A circular coin with diameter \(1\) is dropped onto the square and lands in a random location where the coin is completely contained within the square. The probability that the coin will cover part of the black region of the square can be written as \(\frac{1}{196}\left(a+b\sqrt{2}+\pi\right),\) where \(a\) and \(b\) are positive integers. What is \(a+b?\)

[Figure 1](figures/2021_AMC_10B_Q23_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
Use the usual geometric-probability interpretation: the coin's center is uniformly distributed over all positions that keep the coin inside the square. The coin has radius \(\frac12\), so its center must stay at least \(\frac12\) from every outer edge. Its allowed positions form a square of side \(8-1=7\), with area \(49\).

Place the outer square at \([0,8]\times[0,8]\). The central square diamond has vertices \((4,2)\), \((6,4)\), \((4,6)\), and \((2,4)\). A coin reaches this diamond exactly when its center is inside the diamond or within distance \(\frac12\) of its boundary.

These centers form the diamond itself, four outward rectangles along its sides, and four quarter-disks around its vertices. The pieces have disjoint interiors: outside the diamond, the nearest point lies either on a side or at a vertex. Their total area is
\[
(2\sqrt2)^2
+4(2\sqrt2)\left(\frac12\right)
+\pi\left(\frac12\right)^2
=8+4\sqrt2+\frac\pi4.
\]
This entire region lies inside \([\frac32,\frac{13}{2}]^2\), so none is excluded by the allowed-center square.

Next consider the lower-left black triangle, described by \(x,y\ge0\) and \(x+y\le2\). Its sloping edge makes a \(45^\circ\) angle with the axes. By Pythagoras, moving that edge outward by perpendicular distance \(\frac12\) increases each axis intercept by \(\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\). Thus the relevant parallel boundary is
\[
x+y=2+\frac{\sqrt2}{2}.
\]
Within the allowed-center region, the centers reaching this corner triangle are exactly
\[
x\ge\frac12,\qquad y\ge\frac12,
\qquad x+y\le2+\frac{\sqrt2}{2}.
\]
To check that the finite sloping edge suffices, these inequalities give
\[
|x-y|\le x+y-1
\le1+\frac{\sqrt2}{2}<2.
\]
Hence the perpendicular foot on \(x+y=2\) lies on the actual edge between \((2,0)\) and \((0,2)\). Centers already inside the black triangle also satisfy the displayed inequalities.

The favorable region at this corner is therefore an isosceles right triangle with legs \(1+\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\). All four corners contribute
\[
4\cdot\frac12\left(1+\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)^2
=3+2\sqrt2.
\]

There is no overlap between regions associated with different black components. Distinct corner triangles are at least \(4\) apart. A corner triangle and the central diamond have facing parallel edges separated by \(2\sqrt2\); for example, the lower-left pair lies on \(x+y=2\) and \(x+y=6\). Both distances exceed the coin's diameter \(1\), so one coin cannot reach two different components.

The total favorable center area is
\[
8+4\sqrt2+\frac\pi4+3+2\sqrt2
=11+6\sqrt2+\frac\pi4.
\]
Tangencies and other boundary positions have area zero, so whether touching counts does not change the probability. Under the uniform-center model,
\[
P=\frac{11+6\sqrt2+\pi/4}{49}
=\frac{44+24\sqrt2+\pi}{196}.
\]
Thus \(a=44\), \(b=24\), and \(a+b=\boxed{68}\), choice \(\text{C}\).
solutions.title: Areas of possible coin centers
